racial differences in the rate of change in blood pressure across early childhood are greater for African-American children than for European-American children, and that neighborhood socioeconomic status (as measured by median income and percentage of households receiving public assistance in the neighborhood) accounts for a significant portion of racial differences in the average rate change in blood pressure.

African-American children in the IHDP had higher systolic and di diastolic blood pressures, on average, than European-American children, and that the difference between the two groups was greater for systolic than for diastolic pressure.

understanding the origins of racial disparities in blood pressure and cardiovascular disease.
the role of family and neighborhood socioeconomic status as explanations for racial disparities in cardiovascular health.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
African-American and European American children born preterm have different trajectories of blood pressure across early childhood.
the racial disparity in blood pressure trajectories of preterm children is partially accounted for by neighborhood SES.
the racial disparity in the rate of change in blood pressure among children born preterm is accounted for by the racial disparity in neighborhood SES.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
neighborhood SES is an important factor in the development of blood pressure trajectories in preterm infants, especially among African Americans.
neighborhood SES is an important factor in the early development of racial differences in blood pressures.
the neighborhood environment is a key factor in explaining racial differences in blood pressures in preterm children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neighborhood socioeconomic status, not family socioeconomic status, explains the racial disparity in blood pressure trajectories of preterm children.
racial differences in cardiovascular risk factors emerge early in childhood and that neighborhood socioeconomic status may play an important role in explaining these disparities.
the racial differences we observe are not due to the biological differences between African-Americans and European-Americans.
